courses.title: Physical Pharmacy and Dosage Form Design
courses.description: Solubility and dissolution, rheology, interfacial phenomena, and the formulation of solutions, suspensions, emulsions, tablets and semi-solids.

topics.title: Solubility, Dissolution and Particle Size
topics.summary: Factors affecting solubility, the Noyes–Whitney equation, and particle size reduction.

material.heading: Solubility
material.body: Solubility is the maximum amount of solute that dissolves in a solvent at a given temperature. It depends on the nature of solute and solvent ('like dissolves like'), temperature, pH (for ionisable drugs), crystal form (polymorphs and amorphous forms — the amorphous and metastable forms are more soluble; chloramphenicol palmitate polymorphism affected bioavailability), and additives. Solubility can be improved by salt formation, co-solvents (ethanol, propylene glycol, PEG), surfactant micelles (solubilisation), complexation (cyclodextrins) and pH adjustment.
keyPoints: Improve with salts, co-solvents, surfactants, cyclodextrins

material.heading: Dissolution
material.body: The Noyes–Whitney equation: dC/dt = D·A·(Cs − C)/h, where D is the diffusion coefficient, A the surface area, Cs the saturation solubility, C the concentration in bulk solution and h the diffusion layer thickness. Dissolution rate therefore increases with greater surface area (smaller particles — micronisation, e.g. griseofulvin), higher solubility, stirring (thinner h) and sink conditions. For poorly soluble drugs (BCS Class II), dissolution is rate-limiting for absorption. The Biopharmaceutics Classification System: Class I high solubility/high permeability; II low/high; III high/low; IV low/low.
keyPoints: BCS II: low solubility, high permeability

topics.title: Rheology and Interfacial Phenomena
topics.summary: Newtonian and non-Newtonian flow, thixotropy, surface tension and surfactants.

material.heading: Rheology
material.body: Rheology is the study of flow and deformation. Newtonian fluids (water, simple syrups, glycerol) have constant viscosity regardless of shear rate. Non-Newtonian fluids: plastic (Bingham) systems need a yield stress before flowing (e.g. concentrated suspensions, some ointments); pseudoplastic (shear-thinning) systems become less viscous with increasing shear (polymer solutions such as methylcellulose and tragacanth); dilatant (shear-thickening) systems become more viscous (concentrated deflocculated suspensions). Thixotropy is a time-dependent decrease in viscosity under shear with recovery at rest — desirable in suspensions (thick on standing, pourable when shaken). Viscosity is measured by capillary (Ostwald), falling-sphere or rotational viscometers.

material.heading: Surfaces and surfactants
material.body: Surface tension arises from unbalanced cohesive forces at a liquid surface. Surfactants (surface-active agents) have hydrophilic heads and lipophilic tails; they reduce surface and interfacial tension, form micelles above the critical micelle concentration (CMC), and act as wetting agents, emulsifiers, solubilisers and detergents. They are anionic (sodium lauryl sulphate), cationic (benzalkonium chloride — also antimicrobial), non-ionic (polysorbates/Tweens, sorbitan esters/Spans — low toxicity) or amphoteric (lecithin). The hydrophile–lipophile balance (HLB) scale guides use: 3–6 w/o emulsifiers, 7–9 wetting agents, 8–18 o/w emulsifiers, 13–15 detergents, 15–18 solubilisers.

questions.explanation: Newtonian fluids have constant viscosity.

questions.stem: Polysorbate 80 (Tween 80) is a/an ___ surfactant.
questions.explanation: Tweens are non-ionic polyoxyethylene sorbitan esters.

questions.stem: Sodium lauryl sulphate is an example of a/an ___ surfactant.
questions.explanation: It carries a negatively charged sulphate head.

questions.explanation: Bingham bodies behave as solids below the yield value.

topics.title: Suspensions and Emulsions
topics.summary: Formulation and stability of suspensions and emulsions, Stokes' law and instability types.

material.heading: Suspensions
material.body: A suspension disperses insoluble solid particles in a liquid. Stokes' law: sedimentation velocity v = 2r²(ρs − ρl)g / 9η — so settling slows with smaller particles, closer densities and higher viscosity. Wetting agents help hydrophobic powders disperse; suspending agents (tragacanth, xanthan gum, methylcellulose, bentonite) increase viscosity. Flocculated suspensions (loose aggregates formed by controlled flocculation, e.g. with electrolytes) settle quickly but form a loose, easily redispersed sediment; deflocculated suspensions settle slowly but form a hard 'cake' that is difficult to redisperse. A good suspension settles slowly, redisperses readily and pours easily; label 'Shake well before use'.

material.heading: Emulsions
material.body: An emulsion is a dispersion of one immiscible liquid in another, stabilised by an emulsifying agent. Types: oil-in-water (o/w — miscible with water, washable, used orally and in vanishing creams; dilution test with water, conducts electricity, water-soluble dye colours the continuous phase) and water-in-oil (w/o — greasy, occlusive, e.g. cold creams). Instabilities: creaming (reversible upward/downward concentration of droplets), flocculation, coalescence and cracking (irreversible separation), and phase inversion. Emulsifying agents: surfactants, hydrophilic colloids (acacia, gelatin) and finely divided solids (bentonite). The Bancroft rule: the phase in which the emulsifier is more soluble becomes the continuous phase.

questions.stem: According to Stokes' law, sedimentation rate is proportional to:
questions.explanation: v ∝ r².

questions.stem: Irreversible separation of an emulsion into two layers is called:
questions.explanation: Coalescence leads to cracking, which cannot be reversed by shaking.

questions.stem: Acacia is used in emulsions as a/an:
questions.explanation: Acacia forms a protective film around oil droplets.

questions.stem: Creaming of an emulsion is:
questions.explanation: Droplets remain intact and can be redispersed.

questions.stem: The Bancroft rule states that the continuous phase is the one in which:
questions.explanation: Emulsifier solubility determines emulsion type.

topics.title: Tablets and Capsules
topics.summary: Excipients, granulation, compression, coating, tablet defects and quality control tests.

material.heading: Excipients and manufacture
material.body: Tablet excipients: diluents/fillers (lactose, microcrystalline cellulose, calcium phosphate), binders (starch paste, PVP, gelatin), disintegrants (starch, sodium starch glycolate, croscarmellose — 'superdisintegrants'), lubricants (magnesium stearate — reduces friction with the die; excess slows dissolution), glidants (colloidal silica — improves powder flow) and antiadherents (talc). Manufacturing routes: wet granulation (most common; mixing, wet massing with binder, screening, drying, sizing), dry granulation (slugging or roller compaction — for moisture/heat-sensitive drugs) and direct compression (simplest; needs free-flowing, compressible materials). Coatings: sugar coating, film coating, enteric coating (cellulose acetate phthalate, methacrylate copolymers — dissolve at intestinal pH).

material.heading: Defects and quality control
material.body: Common tablet defects: capping and lamination (separation of the top or layers — entrapped air, excessive fines, too much pressure), picking and sticking (material adhering to punches — moisture, insufficient lubricant), mottling (uneven colour) and chipping. Pharmacopoeial quality tests: uniformity of weight/content, hardness (crushing strength), friability (≤ 1% loss in a Roche friabilator), disintegration time (e.g. uncoated tablets within 15 minutes; film-coated within 30 minutes), and dissolution (e.g. USP basket or paddle apparatus). Capsules are hard gelatin (powders, pellets) or soft gelatin (liquids, oils).

questions.stem: Magnesium stearate is added to tablets as a:
questions.explanation: It reduces friction between the tablet and die wall.

questions.stem: Colloidal silicon dioxide in tablet formulations acts as a:
questions.explanation: It improves powder flow.

questions.stem: Sodium starch glycolate is a:
questions.explanation: It swells rapidly to break tablets apart.

questions.stem: Separation of the top of a tablet from the body is called:
questions.explanation: Capping is often due to entrapped air or excess fines.

questions.stem: Friability of acceptable uncoated tablets should be no more than:
questions.explanation: Weight loss in the friabilator should not exceed 1%.

questions.stem: The granulation method used for moisture- and heat-sensitive drugs is:
questions.explanation: Dry granulation avoids liquid and heat.

questions.stem: Enteric coating polymers dissolve at:
questions.explanation: They resist stomach acid and dissolve in the intestine.

questions.stem: Oily liquids such as vitamin E are commonly filled into:
questions.explanation: Soft gelatin capsules hold liquids and oils.

topics.title: Semi-solids, Suppositories and Parenterals
topics.summary: Ointment and cream bases, suppository bases, and formulation of injections.

material.heading: Semi-solids and suppositories
material.body: Ointment bases: hydrocarbon (oleaginous) bases such as white soft paraffin — occlusive, emollient, not water-washable; absorption bases (wool fat/lanolin, which can absorb water); water-removable (emulsifying ointment) bases; and water-soluble bases (macrogols/PEG). Creams are semi-solid emulsions (o/w vanishing creams, w/o cold creams) and generally need preservatives. Pastes contain a high proportion of powder (e.g. zinc oxide paste). Gels are semi-solid systems with gelling agents (carbomer). Suppository bases: fatty bases (theobroma oil/cocoa butter — melts at body temperature; polymorphic, must not be overheated; hard fat/Witepsol) and water-soluble bases (glycerol–gelatin, macrogols — dissolve in rectal fluid, can irritate). Displacement value is used to calculate base quantities.
keyPoints: Cocoa butter melts at body temperature; avoid overheating

material.heading: Parenterals
material.body: Parenteral products must be sterile, pyrogen-free, free of visible particles, and ideally isotonic and at physiological pH. Vehicles: water for injections (most), fixed oils for depot IM injections (e.g. some hormones, antipsychotics). Isotonicity can be adjusted with sodium chloride or dextrose (calculated by freezing-point depression — 0.9% NaCl and 5% dextrose are iso-osmotic with plasma, freezing point −0.52 °C). Large-volume parenterals (infusions) must not contain preservatives; multidose vials must. Ampoules are single-use glass containers; vials have rubber closures. Particulate matter and incompatibilities (e.g. precipitation of calcium phosphate) must be avoided in admixtures.

options: Formation of unstable polymorphs that fail to set properly
questions.explanation: Unstable polymorphs have lower melting points.

questions.stem: Which solution is isotonic with plasma?
questions.explanation: 0.9% NaCl has the same osmotic pressure as plasma.

questions.stem: The freezing point of plasma used for isotonicity calculations is:
questions.explanation: Solutions freezing at −0.52 °C are isotonic.

questions.stem: Large-volume intravenous infusions must NOT contain:
questions.explanation: Large volumes of preservative would be toxic.

questions.explanation: Pastes are stiff and protective.
